The Bahama swallow (Tachycineta cyaneoviridis) is a small, iridescent passerine endemic to the pine forests of the northern Bahamas. Field observations indicate that this species exhibits a relatively standard clutch size for a tropical aerial insectivore. Females typically produce three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three eggs per clutch], and available data suggest that they raise a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This modest annual reproductive output is characteristic of many island-dwelling hirundinids. The initial wet weight of a newly laid egg is estimated at 2 grams [Ww0 = 2 grams], representing a considerable parental investment relative to the female's own body mass and reflecting the rich yolk reserves required to sustain the developing embryo. Eggs are incubated for a period that is highly dependent on local thermal conditions. Under controlled incubation protocols maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at birth, marking the moment of hatching, is recorded as approximately 15.8 days [ab = approximately 15.8 days]. This incubation duration aligns with values reported for other Tachycineta species of comparable egg size.

Following a successful hatching event, the altricial nestlings emerge with a body weight that is notably modest. The wet weight at birth is about 1.8 grams [Wwb = about 1.8 grams]. This low neonatal mass places the chicks in a vulnerable phase of parental dependency, requiring frequent provisioning from both adults to sustain rapid growth. Nestlings grow quickly within the cavity nest, fueled by a diet of insects delivered continuously throughout the day. The developmental trajectory culminates in a critical life-history transition when the young birds achieve their first flight. Under the thermal regime typical of the swallow's active metabolic season, which centers on a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at fledging has been documented at 22.7 days [tx = 22.7 days]. This age at nest departure is shorter than that observed in some temperate Tachycineta species, potentially an adaptation to the subtropical climate and predation pressures.

As the fledgling enters the juvenile stage, it must rapidly acquire the skills necessary for independent foraging. The period between fledging and the attainment of a fully adult body mass is characterized by refinement of flight maneuvers and insect capture techniques. The species ultimately reaches an ultimate wet weight in adulthood of 17.7 grams [Wwi = 17.7 grams], a value that is consistent across both sexes and appears to be a robust indicator of a healthy individual within the population. This adult mass is achieved within a few weeks after leaving the nest. The subsequent trajectory toward reproductive competence unfolds over a longer timescale. At the same thermoneutral body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated to be 68.1 days [tp = 68.1 days]. This relatively early onset of gonadal maturation is notable, yet actual breeding is typically delayed until the following breeding season, presumably due to constraints related to territory establishment and social maturity.

The first reproductive event for an individual Bahama swallow does not usually coincide with its first physiological opportunity to breed. Most yearlings do not attempt to nest, instead deferring their first clutch until the subsequent calendar year. The time since birth at first brood has been recorded at approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days], marking the production of the initial clutch. at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]This deferral of reproduction for nearly a full year after reaching physiological maturity is a common life-history tactic among tropical passerines, allowing young birds to gain critical experience and secure a high-quality nesting cavity. All of these developmental and reproductive metrics occur under the physiological baseline of an active endotherm operating at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This elevated and stable internal temperature is a prerequisite for the rapid enzymatic processes driving growth, feather synthesis, and muscle development. The species exhibits a relatively short lifespan typical of small passerines, with maximum recorded longevity in the wild estimated at about 9.1 years [am = about 9.1 years] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

The population dynamics of the Bahama swallow are influenced by a combination of its reproductive schedule and its vulnerability to stochastic environmental events, such as hurricanes. Given that a female produces only a single brood of three eggs each year, the annual reproductive rate is limited. This low annual output underscores the importance of adult survival for maintaining stable population numbers. The maximum reproductive rate, consisting of three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three eggs per clutch] and one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], means that even small increases in adult mortality can have pronounced negative effects on the population growth rate. Research into the ecological drivers of this species' life history is ongoing, with particular interest in how food availability in the pine forest ecosystem modulates the timing of breeding and the condition of nestlings. Field studies continue to refine estimates of key parameters, with banding data providing robust evidence for the 9.1-year maximum lifespan and the age-dependent patterns of first reproduction. Future work should focus on quantifying the impact of cavity availability on the realized reproductive output of this endemic species.
